entries.title: Upland by Ed Douglas review – a glorious survey of Britain’s high places
entries.summary: The writer and climber brings colour and carnival to his account of a country and people shaped by its mountainsIt comes as a shock to learn that Britain’s uplands were not always rocky, covered with coarse grass and suitable only for sheep. entries.content:
It comes as a shock to learn that Britain’s uplands were not always rocky, covered with coarse grass and suitable only for sheep. About 54,000 years ago – a mere blink in geological time – this island’s high places were teeming with nature. Lushly forested peaks, crags and gorges were home to megafauna including mammoth, woolly rhinoceros and giant elk. The one sour note in this elevated Garden of Eden was the carnivorous cave lions and sabre-tooth cats who prowled the browse looking for a meaty dinner.

Ed Douglas’s achievement in this excellent book is to return a proper sense of colour and even carnival to Britain’s high places. His first job, though, is to define his terms. In 1936, the celebrated US geographer Roderick Peattie declared that what made a mountain was not its elevation so much as its capacity to “enter into the imagination of the people who lived in [its] shadows”. But by the 1990s, the United Nations, newly tasked with protecting the world’s high places from environmental and economic decline, insisted on getting out its tape measure and statistical charts and coming up with some universal criteria.

Consequently, the current definition of a “mountainous” region is one where the altitude varies by at least 300 metres over a radius of 7km. That means that Douglas’s home on Totley Moor, which sits on the millstone grit uplands of the eastern Peak District, just about qualifies; a matter of obvious satisfaction to this one-time editor of the Alpine Journal. Romping comfortably across the line are whole swathes of Scotland, Wales and northern England, not forgetting the twin domes of Exmoor and Dartmoor.

Less pleasing to Douglas, though, is the way in which Britain’s uplands have historically been imagined as places apart, spectacular yet oddly detached from life at lower levels. He reminds us that the country’s high places provide more than 60% of the nation’s water needs. What’s more, the plants that make up much of our diet originate in that same hardy environment: potatoes, barley, maize, apples, tomatoes. Those of us who live at sea level or below would do well to reformulate our ideas about the uplands as a place where nothing much grows beyond the occasional sprig of lucky heather.

Equally misguided, suggests Douglas, is a tendency to view Britain’s uplands as existing outside history, politics, culture and even time itself. The truth is that mountains have shaped much of our island story. When the Romans arrived from mainland Europe in the first century AD, they found that low-lying southern England, with its fertile soil and gentle hillocks, quickly rolled over and signed up to the new order. The craggy north, meanwhile, stood aloof – and you can still see evidence of this bifurcated response in the landscape today. Go to a Roman ruin in the south or east of the country, and chances are that it is the remnants of a country estate or, at the very least, a handsome villa. Head to the high north and you will find yourself scrambling over the remains of a garrison or high brick wall aimed at keeping uplanders away from the good stuff.

And yet … it frequently turns out that it was precisely in those cold, difficult and, above all, lofty places that actual treasure lay. The Romans eventually overcame their fear of heights to start mining lead in Wanlockhead, which at more than 400 metres remains Scotland’s highest village. A thousand years later and the Norman invaders, who had initially given the rocky spine of England a wide berth, set up shop in the Peak District and insisted on taking a cut of the handsome profits that arose from local lead mining.

Douglas suggests that the best way to think of this ceaseless push and pull between the central lowlands and the marginal uplands is as a kind of internal colonialism. For millennia, Britain’s high places have been ransacked for their raw materials. Perhaps the most poignant example in this book is the story of the Elan valley, a beautiful stretch of land in the mountains of rural mid-Wales. In the early 19th century the poet Percy Shelley had roamed over his uncle’s Radnorshire estate, entranced to have found his own version of Wordsworth and Coleridge’s Lake District.

But in 1896, the valley was dammed and flooded in order to create a vast reservoir from which Birmingham might draw an everlasting supply of cheap and clean drinking water. It was part of the MP Joseph Chamberlain’s radical programme to clear England’s second city of cholera and dysentery by building a 73-mile aqueduct from the Welsh mountains to the Midlands plateau. This necessitated the village of Nantgwyllt, complete with church and surrounding farms, disappearing permanently under water.

The compulsory purchase of the Elan valley carries echoes of the earlier Highland clearances, during which tenant farmers in Sutherland, Argyll and Inverness-shire were ordered off the land to make way for the infinitely more profitable sheep. Many of these evicted crofters, just like the Radnorshire farmers 150 years later, were obliged to emigrate as far as the US to find a place to build a stable home.

Yet it would be doomy and defeatist to suggest that the uplands have exclusively been places of passive trauma. Douglas does a good job at identifying those times throughout history when Britain’s high places demonstrated a culture of determined resistance. There are the Jacobite rebellions of 1715 and 1745 when Highlanders loyal to the Stuart cause swept down from their mountain fastness in an attempt to overthrow the newly installed Hanoverians. This tartan army got as far as Derby, only 110 miles from London, before being forced to turn back.

Douglas has not, in truth, found out anything new about the ancient uplands, but he has knitted his sources into a deft survey, going all the way from the tectonic plates of prehistory to today, when the chief concern is southern second-homers driving up the prices for young locals. One delight of his capacious, looping narrative is the room it leaves for delightful cameos by remarkable individuals, including several women.

There is Janet Lapworth, the daughter of a Galashiels schoolteacher, who in the 1870s sewed her geologist husband a special waistcoat incorporating rows of pockets on the front into which he could sort his specimens on the fly. Or Hannah Mitchell, who grew up on a hard-scrabble tenant farm with a view of Kinder Scout, the highest point in the Peak District, and developed a love of rambling to offset the constricted conditions of her own impoverished life. Mitchell’s determination to walk off her troubles led to her becoming a suffragette, a JP and a campaigner for social justice.

My favourite uplander, though, remains Queen Victoria. As a young girl she gorged on the highly confected Highland novels of Walter Scott. Now that Jacobitism was safely defeated, it was delightful to imagine a Highlands full of craggily handsome men in kilts ready to come a lady’s rescue, even if that lady happened to be a Protestant Hanoverian princess. When she bought Balmoral in 1852, the queen was not initially much interested in venturing far. But with the death of Albert she was persuaded to undertake the occasional excursion up famous peaks including Lochnagar and Ben Macdui. Here was the beginning of what the 20th-century novelist George Scott-Moncrieff memorably called “Balmorality”. It was a view of the uplands, spruced up and watered down, best seen on a biscuit tin.

entries.title: Underdogs by Louise Powell review – a powerful debut with plenty of northern soul
entries.summary: A bereaved father and son bond over greyhound racing in an east Durham town in terminal declineThe adjoining villages of Easington and Easington Colliery in the coalfields of east Durham make the perfect case study of the shift from England’s industrial boomtime to terminal decline. entries.content:
The adjoining villages of Easington and Easington Colliery in the coalfields of east Durham make the perfect case study of the shift from England’s industrial boomtime to terminal decline. Twenty miles from a major town or city, they’ve been left to languish ever since Thatcher went to war with the industry that made them. If you want to understand why the white working class feel abandoned today, go to Easington Colliery and its surrounding villages.

It’s this community that Middlesbrough-born writer Louise Powell brings to life in a powerful debut set in the world of greyhound racing, or “flapping”. Underdogs is an utterly authentic depiction of an England that’s overlooked, but still very much alive. Pigeon lofts and flat caps, meat raffles and social clubs – all still exist, just very rarely in 21st-century novels.

Ten-year-old George Wheatley and his broken father Reg, both grieving the loss of George’s mother, who died two years earlier, are drawn into the dog-track culture by charismatic ex-miner Bertie, who despite the “half-pint of black phlegm he hawked up off his lungs every mornin’” decides not to pursue an incapacity benefit claim as he can make better money rinsing out the various illegal bookmakers by racing his dogs. When the bookies refuse to take Bertie’s bets he ropes in those down on their luck to race his dogs for him, and hands over his bitch Goldie, “twenny-nine kilo of muscles coiled like springs … a Ferrari of an engine in her fawn chest and a nose that could been made by Concorde”. Scores of those on the breadline have benefited from Bertie’s hustle.

The love that George feels for Goldie is matched only by his need to survive in an uncompromising adult world where the greatest threat comes from aggrieved bookmaker Baz, who has designs on their prized canine charge. Powell is strongest when describing the details of track life, a seemingly simple pursuit given a dark edge by the high-stakes money changing hands and further complicated by the treatment of these graceful creatures who are bred and discarded for human amusement and profit.

That the novel is set in 1998 is significant; all of County Durham’s pits had finally closed, but major regeneration investment was on its way from local boy Tony Blair, with his talk of “regional task forces” and “enterprise zones”. Old slag piles were soon to became nature reserves and pithead monuments. A bright new future was promised, though it’s barely glimpsed here; today Easington has one of the whitest demographics in the country (currently 98.4%), and was the place worst hit by 2025 disability allowance cuts.

Here, then, is a hard-scratch existence based around family alliances and power struggles in the dying days of an analogue world, where scars received from police truncheons at Orgreave are shown and shared, and where premature death stalks the terraced streets. George and Reg emerge as tender and quietly heroic; the father’s grief for his lost wife is almost overwhelming at times, as are the reminders of George’s malnutrition. This is real first-world poverty, as it still exists today. During the second world war British-based fascist William Joyce, better known as Lord Haw-Haw, remarked that “the people of Easington will be eating greyhounds, not raising them”; he sorely underestimated just how much the English love their dogs, and it’s no coincidence that Powell’s descriptions of the greyhound’s meals are more mouthwatering than anything father and son eat.

North-east writers of literary fiction have always had plenty to sing about, but not much in the way of support from the publishing industry; “too bleak” and “too northern” are words familiar to many of us from the region. Given the rich cultural tradition of storytelling and folk song, always told in distinctively melodic vernacular voices, this still feels like an oversight. With recent novels from Eliza Clark, Glen James Brown, Jessica Andrews and Lucy Rose all finding critical favour, it’s clear that there are infinite Englands in existence. And as Underdogs movingly demonstrates, it’s these untold stories that need to be on the page – now more than ever.

Benjamin Myers’s most recent novel is Jesus Christ Kinski (Bloomsbury).

entries.title: Gaining Ground by Joan Barfoot review – Anne Enright celebrates a landmark feminist novel
entries.summary: Half a century on, this tale of a woman who abandons her children in search of her self remains thrillingly originalThere is a growing literature of maternal flight: novels about women who leave not just their husbands but also the children they have made. In the real world, men are the more frequent deserters; the connection of the father to family life is seen as contingent, while motherhood is
entries.content:
There is a growing literature of maternal flight: novels about women who leave not just their husbands but also the children they have made. In the real world, men are the more frequent deserters; the connection of the father to family life is seen as contingent, while motherhood is revered as an intrinsic state. This means that women who “un-mother” themselves are doing something impossible: the connection between a woman and her child is not just emotional, but also creational. Joan Barfoot understands the inside-out nature of the logic involved in maternal obligation: “she created these other people and their need for her,” says Abra, the abandoning mother of Gaining Ground, “and now she must fulfil them.”

Abra neglects to fulfil her children or their needs. The novel is rigorously and meditatively about the business of separation, which is also the business of becoming a single and undivided self.

Gaining Ground came out in Canada in 1978, under the title Abra, before it was published in the UK under the current title by the Women’s Press in 1980. This was around the time Barfoot’s fellow Canadian Alice Munro began to write her adulterous, runaway women, whose instinct for freedom chimed so well with the feminism of the day. Abra is not sprung from domesticity by her desire for another man, however, nor does she return to her children, as Leda in Elena Ferrante’s The Lost Daughter does, after years spent regaining what she had lost. Abra is closer to the protagonist in Cathy Sweeney’s recent Breakdown, who has no single answer to the question of why she left her former life: In Japan, Sweeney writes, “So many people disappear that there is a word for them – johatsu. It translates as evaporated people.”

These novels cannot fully resist the question of whether the bolting mother is a monster or a victim of societal expectation. Gaining Ground was written before any of them and, already, Barfoot was wise enough to refuse the terms of the debate: Abra never questions the morality of becoming her true self.

The novel begins with the arrival of a young woman at Abra’s cabin in the woods, nine years after she drove away from her old life. Abra feels her presence as a pressure, an expectation, but can barely remember who the girl is, or who she herself used to be. Then, a moment of recognition – it is her 18-year-old daughter, Katie: “I know her now, and it locks me to her.”

Katie’s arrival tips Abra into a recollection of her lovely, ordered home in Toronto; her marriage, in which there would sometimes be “late movies and making love on the couch and popcorn”; and her two children. Her first baby, a son, provoked a fierce sense of attachment: “I didn’t even want to talk about him, although he so completely occupied my mind, because I felt somehow that talking about him took him a distance away, made him separate, gave a piece of him to someone else.” Her second child seemed less of a miracle: “she was a baby, beautiful, and she was mine and Stephen’s and we had created her, but it seemed natural now”.

The story may be about maternal ambivalence, depression, the loss of meaning, but it always revolves around ideas of truth and pretence. Abra’s life does not feel “real”. Barfoot delivers about 16 different kinds of dissociation without going over her own footprints or saying the same thing twice. The build to Abra’s departure has a cumulative, relentless modernist effect, but she manages to keep it human, or within the human, and we are fully convinced, when Abra sees the cabin for the first time, that this is her “home”.

She has brought no clocks and no mirror, and is at pains to avoid talking to other people. On her first day of digging a vegetable garden her hair proves bothersome and so she lops it off, blind. Abra works to grow food, gather wood and keep herself alive through the long Canadian winter. She thinks only about what is in front of her. The descriptions of work, the natural world and the changing seasons recall the self-reliance of Annie Dillard or Thoreau, who write in a transcendent spiritual tradition. Abra’s revelation is not about God’s infinite majesty, however, but about a kind of unbecoming. She wants to make a life in which she can slowly lose “my name, my memory, the labels I’d used, and so my sense of all words”, to arrive at a place of joy.

When Katie arrives from a world where “there are motives and angers everywhere”, Abra tries to share what she has discovered about “blankness”. She considers the way she once saw her husband and wonders, “Did I make him up?” The answer is that she invented everyone: “I simplified them. And then I reacted to what I had made up, behaved as if what I had invented was real.”

It is hard to find an ending for a book that is trying to be about nothing, so it is considerably to her credit that Barfoot manages an affecting, dramatic conclusion to Katie’s visit. Gaining Ground is a wonderful slow burn of a book and Barfoot’s originality and control remain exciting, nearly half a century on. It is great to see this reissue put the novel at the centre of things, where it belongs.

entries.title: What If We Got AI Right? by Eleanor Drage review – avoiding apocalypse
entries.summary: The academic’s ambitious guide to the ethics of tech falls short of its promise to provide meaningful answersThe AI ethicist Eleanor Drage believes that to thrive alongside artificial intelligence, humans need to recognise AI’s “humanity”. She means that while we often speak of AI as though it were some mystical, formless thing, it is the product of hours of human labour, in silicon and quartz min
entries.content:
The AI ethicist Eleanor Drage believes that to thrive alongside artificial intelligence, humans need to recognise AI’s “humanity”. She means that while we often speak of AI as though it were some mystical, formless thing, it is the product of hours of human labour, in silicon and quartz mines, microchip factories and data labelling centres. If citizens want to wrest power from the tech companies that are building AI, it helps to understand clearly what they are selling us. This also means seeing through the marketing and hype: “the cloud”, that nebulous, distant place where your photos are stored, is just someone else’s computer; an AI “hallucination” is a system error or data labelling mistake; intelligence is a very broad – and potentially misleading – term.

The story in Silicon Valley is that AI will either save us, ushering in a new era of prosperity and human longevity, or it will wipe us all out. Drage argues, convincingly, that big tech cannot possibly deliver on its utopian promises while it continues to chase profit and power above all else, and while it serves the interests of a narrow few. Meanwhile, the cultural obsession with the AI-induced apocalypse conveniently redirects attention from the practical conversations we could be having about how to make AI safer – by ensuring citizens have more power over how their information is used, and how AI models are trained and regulated, for example. Tech titans’ apocalyptic visions also create the false impression that AI safety is more important than climate change, geopolitical tensions and inequality, three problems that are already causing a huge amount of suffering and that, if addressed, would reduce many AI-linked risks too.

Drage, an assistant research professor at the University of Cambridge’s Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence, has conducted research that debunks AI-powered recruitment processes, and exposes the dangers of incorporating AI into law enforcement. Many of her criticisms of big tech will be familiar: that AI algorithms perpetuate and entrench pre-existing biases; that for all their bland, generic promises to be “transparent” and “accountable”, tech giants have become too big to care about ethics; that a handful of executives have amassed far too much power; and that the rollout of AI is happening without our consent and without consideration for planetary health. But her writing has intellectual heft, and her philosophical explorations of, for example, how we define intelligence and why this matters, are very interesting.

Occasionally, however, Drage’s arguments seem rushed and become sloppy. “It’s merely an illusion that the labour force is disappearing: work is simply shifting, from artists to data labellers and from marketeers to engineers,” she writes at one point. But it’s not clear that artists and “marketeers” will become redundant in the coming AI era. It’s also not as though the data labellers working for poverty wages in Kenya would have been artists 10 years ago. Equally, given the importance she rightly places on promoting diversity in AI, it’s disappointing that she dismisses unconscious bias as “merely another way of taking the perspective of the perpetrator rather than the recipient of harm”, as though intention is completely irrelevant. She writes that people are ready for “less placid” conversations about equality, I’d add that these conversations also demand accuracy and nuance.

The book’s title suggests Drage wants to offer an alternative vision of what AI could be. She gives a few examples of the kind of ethical, community-based AI projects she thinks should be replacing top-down big tech products, and many of them are strangely underwhelming. They include an app called Mumkin designed to facilitate difficult conversations about female genital mutilation (FGM) in India, and Kuini, an AI chatbot built to help Māori women quit smoking. In both instances I found myself wondering what value AI brings to these endeavours – particularly given all that Drage has discussed about its environmental impact and exploitative supply chains. Is an app more effective than training community members to act as counsellors, or funding support groups and peer support workers?

Drage describes a toolkit she co-designed to help AI companies act ethically and comply with EU regulations as a “cornerstone of utopianism”, because it shifts the focus on to how AI is built and made. In her view, utopia is not a destination but the “process of working together to develop a fairer world”. Maybe it would be unfair to expect too specific a utopian vision, but I’d nonetheless be interested to know how AI, specifically, can help us build a better future. She does not mention the things that many of AI’s biggest critics nonetheless welcome, such as its potential to improve drug discovery and disease detection. What if we got AI right, this book asks. After reading it, I can’t say I really know.

entries.title: From author to anime hero: the unlikely revival of a Japanese literary star
entries.summary: More than seven decades after they were first released, the dark novels of Osamu Dazai have become a publishing sensation, as a new generation of readers engage with his bleakness, humour and brillianceThere’s no question that Japanese literature has been one of the outstanding successes for British bookshops in recent years: in 2024 close to half of the bestselling translated fiction titles were
entries.content:
There’s no question that Japanese literature has been one of the outstanding successes for British bookshops in recent years: in 2024 close to half of the bestselling translated fiction titles were from Japan. Much of the Japanese fiction translated into English fits into broad categories – cats, crime, coffee shops – but one surprise bestseller stands alone.

Sales of books by Osamu Dazai, who killed himself in 1948 aged 38, have rocketed in the last few years. His best-known novel, No Longer Human (1948), has sold more than 75,000 copies in the UK alone. An intense semi-autobiographical account of one man’s alienation, it was the last work of fiction completed before Dazai’s death.

Born in the north of Japan in 1909 to a wealthy family, Dazai was a brilliant student, but showed early signs of mental ill health, making two suicide attempts by the age of 21. He lived what his translator Donald Keene called a “life of wild dissipation”, including morphine addiction and a number of relationships.

Until recently, Dazai’s work has been available only in imported editions from the US publisher New Directions. But this month, Penguin Classics capitalises on his unexpected popularity by publishing the first UK edition of Dazai’s work in almost 70 years: a collection of short stories from a female perspective, titled Schoolgirl.

Polly Barton, who selected and translated the stories into English, tells me that, although Dazai may be relatively new to English-speaking readers, in Japan, he is “one of the big three, along with Yukio Mishima and Ryūnosuke Akutagawa, that everyone talks about as the fathers of modern Japanese literature”.

In recent years, Barton adds, he has been discovered by a new generation of younger readers. “The sense I get is that he’s particularly popular with young men – the demographic that we’re constantly told is not reading books.” This is even more surprising, since Dazai’s novels are not traditional bestseller material. They are bleak, nihilistic and riddled with their narrators’ self-loathing.

No Longer Human comprises a series of notebooks by a formerly “handsome young man”, who declares his incompatibility with the human race. For him, the world is “a place of bottomless horror”; he concludes that “living itself is the source of sin”. The narrator of the title story of Schoolgirl takes a similar view: “the problem is that I’m corrupt. I’m a bad girl.”

The relentless pessimism in Dazai’s work risks seeming overwhelming or indulgent but, as Barton puts it, Dazai “leans into [the self-loathing] with a kind of exuberance”. Indeed, his appeal in part lies in this “unashamed emotional quality, but also tempered with enormous intelligence”.

Tynan Kogane, the editor-in-chief at New York-based New Directions, agrees. “I think a lot of young readers see themselves in Dazai’s works.” He adds that “there’s a lot of nihilism and despair in Dazai’s work, and it’s unfortunate for our country at the moment, but there’s a lot of nihilism and despair [here too]. The unhappy man in postwar Japan really resonates with a lot of readers.”

Dazai’s popularity among younger readers may have spread online – on Reddit and TikTok, where commenters praise him as the only person that understands me”. But his renaissance also has unexpected roots in a 2016 Japanese anime TV series called Bungo Stray Dogs, which has fictionalised versions of real writers as its central characters.

This bizarre series, featuring a “swashbuckling” version of Osamu Dazai, has been a godsend for book sales, says Chris Wait, an editor at New Directions. Soon after the TV series was released in America in 2018, New Directions noticed sales of Dazai’s books growing.

“Before that we were selling dozens or hundreds of copies [a year],” Kogane says. As Bungo Stray Dogs fever grew, Dazai’s sales went stratospheric. “At the height of it,” Wait adds, “the annual figure was something like 150,000 copies, which for us is pretty rare.” Is it true that sales of No Longer Human bought New Directions a new office floor? “Yes,” replies Wait. “And our previous carpeting was very much in need of an update.”

But the appeal of Dazai’s work goes much further than this cartoon cameo. His books have both style and substance. There’s “a natural gregariousness to his storytelling,” Wait says, “this raconteurship that keeps you reading no matter what he’s talking about”.

Beyond the heartfelt despair of No Longer Human, novellas such as The Flowers of Buffoonery (1935) and The Beggar Student (1940) are frequently playful and funny; self-referential and self-mocking. “Why do I bother writing novels?” the narrator of The Beggar Student asks. “Am I lured by the glory of literary celebrity? Or do I simply want to write bestsellers and cash huge cheques? Let me spare you the theatrics. I want both. So bad it hurts.”

Similarly, Schoolgirl, with its exclusively female viewpoints, presents a different side to Dazai. The authenticity of the voice may be in part because the title story, as Barton tells me, “was heavily based on the diary of a real 19-year-old schoolgirl that Dazai was sent in the post”.

But Dazai’s most famous book remains inextricably linked with his own life – and death. In No Longer Human, the narrator has survived a suicide pact in which his girlfriend died. Soon after finishing the book, Dazai completed his own suicide pact with his lover Tomie Yamazaki. Their bodies were recovered six days later, on what would have been his 39th birthday. But his work – now more than ever – lives on.

Schoolgirl by Osamu Dazai, translated by Polly Barton, is published by Penguin Classics. To order a copy go to guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

entries.title: The perfect books for the beach … picked by Freida McFadden, Mick Herron, Robert Harris and more
entries.summary: From a transporting historical saga to a tale of small-town betrayal, the authors of our favourite page-turners reveal the books they take on holiday – introduced by Jenny ColganIt is important to follow a balanced diet on holiday. Too many “My Wife’s Sister’s Husband’s Psychopath”, and you’ll get confused and grumpy. Too much sugary romance and your teeth will fall out. Something too big and chal
entries.content:
It is important to follow a balanced diet on holiday. Too many “My Wife’s Sister’s Husband’s Psychopath”, and you’ll get confused and grumpy. Too much sugary romance and your teeth will fall out. Something too big and challenging you’ve been meaning to get round to for ages will make you feel guilty and more liable to give in to scrolling, and if you take too many supposedly upmarket “must reads” of the summer, you will simply prove to yourself just how much overhyped averageness there is out there, when all you want is something satisfying.

You need to be able to chop and change depending on your mood, which means fiction and nonfiction. And finally, you need to be able to throw all of these rules out of the window if you find a sandy old water-stained copy of, for example, James Herbert’s Domain in your holiday cottage and decide to devote yourself to 600 pages of post-nuclear mutant rat-strewn London, or choose to go for a full-on Maeve Binchy sesh.

My top tips for this summer? For the outward journey: Kathy Burke’s smash-hit and brilliant autobiography A Mind of My Own, a reminder of the absolute Britishness you are leaving behind. For that first post-rosé afternoon when you are filled with warmth and benevolence towards the world and everyone in it: Whistler by Ann Patchett.

For a wonderful immersive epic where everyone is also extremely boiling hot all the time: This Is Where the Serpent Lives by Daniyal Mueenuddin. For cruising altitude day four when everyone else has gone to see some stupid boring hot cave and left you alone and you want something quality and capable of being finished in an afternoon: Glorious Exploits by Ferdia Lennon. For the day everyone is doing your head in: Emma Cline’s huge hit from a couple of years ago, The Guest, a thoroughly nasty piece of work and the best of all those “neighbourhood psycho” books.

Nonfiction palate cleanser day: OK, everyone is going to be reading the Maggie Haberman Trump book, but for the love of God could we possibly not think about him for one solitary five-second interval? That would be the definition of a holiday. If annoying Americans are still your bag, try Belle Burden’s Strangers, about a seemingly perfect, rich Wasp marriage unexpectedly going down the toilet.

For queueing at non-EU passport control and cursing Nigel Farage’s £5m: The Impossible Fortune by Richard Osman. Forget the motley crew of celebrity impersonators that squelched along in his wake; Osman’s lightness of touch and genuine comic ability means this slips down more easily than free limoncello. Bonnes vacances!

Freida McFadden

author of The Housemaid

One of my favourite reads of the year has been TheCalamity Clubby Kathryn Stockett. I’ve been on a historical kick lately, and this novel set in the southern US during the Great Depression is historical fiction at its best. The audiobook is masterfully narrated and by the last chapter, I had tears in my eyes.

Caro Claire Burke

author of Yesteryear

In The Shampoo Effect by Jenny Jackson a group of friends in their mid-30s in a tight-knit Massachusetts coastal town deal with secrets, romance and the fallout from a stunning betrayal. It’s frothy and clever and perfect for a vacation.

Taffy Brodesser-Akner

author of Fleishman Is in Trouble

I brought Here in the Dark by my New York Times colleague Alexis Soloski on vacation a couple of years ago. I couldn’t put it down from the minute I started it, even missing a family dinner so I could continue reading. (Sorry, kids!) It’s a modern noir about an acerbic theatre critic who finds herself caught up in a mystery, and I can’t say enough about its voice, its humour, its darkness, its poignancy and the twists and turns that make it a truly original thriller. I loved it.

Alice Oseman

author of HeartstopperConvenience Store Woman by Sayaka Murata is about a woman whose only dream is to work at a convenience store and, like much of Murata’s work, explores the inner world of a woman who feels deeply uncomfortable about the role she’s forced into by society. It’s short, it’s strange, it’s the perfect read for a trip away this summer – and a great introduction to Murata, if you haven’t dipped in before.

Mick Herron

author of the Slough House series

Beaches are for walking along not reading on, but when the paddling’s done and a sand-free environment’s been found, Daniel Mason’s Country People is a treat. A failed academic and his family relocate to Vermont, where his PhD avoidance strategies involve increasingly alarming immersion in local folklore. An absurd, joyful delight.

Nita Prose

author of The MaidThe Paper Palace by Miranda Cowley Heller. August heat, a summer cabin in Cape Cod, and the unravelling of one woman’s secrets. Elle is happily married with three kids, but her whole life is upended by an illicit encounter with a childhood friend. A charged generational saga about love, desire and loss – you’ll need regular dips in the water to cool yourself as you read.

Lisa Jewell

author of None of This Is True

The best page-turner I’ve read this year is It’s Not What You Thinkby Clare Mackintosh. She already lays claim to one of the genre’s greatest twists in her 2011 hit I Let You Go and here Mackintosh is back to deliver multiple twists, short chapters and non-stop reveals in this scintillating read.

André Aciman

author of Call Me by Your NameLondon Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe is about a 19-year-old Londoner who desperately wants to join the world of super-wealthy Russian oligarchs, many of whom live in the capital. He manages to affect belonging to that class until he is finally exposed for who he really is – a smart, resourceful but hapless kid. The story is totally addictive, real, and I couldn’t put it down.

Lucy Foley

author of The Guest ListThe Wedding People by Alison Espach is an absorbing, transporting book that left me with a serious what-to-pick-next panic after finishing it. I took it on holiday last year and the summer setting makes it perfect: the waterfront hotel, the excursions on boats and in open-top cars, and also the unfurling sense of optimism. It’s a paean to solo travel, to leaving it – quite literally in this case – all behind. But it’s also a book with teeth, poignancy, depth and humanity, all qualities I look for in a top-notch summer read.

Erin Kelly

author of The Night StairsThe Pinnacle by Abir Mukherjee is a satirical thriller set in a Mumbai skyscraper. A washed-up American actor is accused of killing his Bollywood starlet wife. It’s got everything you could want from a book: belly laughs, unforgettable characters, a thumping plot and simmering political rage.

Leigh Bardugo

author of the Ninth House seriesThe Last Baron by Tom Sancton. Thick with loathsome individuals and rich with history, this heavily researched story of a 1970s kidnapping in Paris spans generations. It is wildly juicy, just be prepared for a Succession experience: you’ll struggle to find anyone to root for but you won’t be able to look away.

Matt Haig

author of The Midnight LibraryThe Infinite Sadness of Small Appliances by Glenn Dixon is a weird, wonderful book about a vacuum cleaner that becomes sentient after hearing To Kill a Mockingbird read aloud. Said vacuum cleaner renames herself Scout and embarks on a quest to save the human she lives with. It’s highly original and feels like a sign that – in the age of AI – the way out is through vivid human creativity.

Florence Knapp

author of The Names

A will-they-won’t-they romance is a much-anticipated holiday treat for me, and Annabel Monaghan’s are guaranteed to make my cheeks ache from smiling and keep me reading until 2am. In Nora Goes Off Script, screenwriter and single mum Nora falls for a leading actor when her house is co-opted as a film location.

Robert Harris

author of Conclave

Graham Greene has accompanied me on a lot of holidays over the years, especially the novels set in hot climates. I recommend in particular The Power and the Glory, The Honorary Consuland The Quiet American – perfect reading for a sweltering beach, a deserted baggage hall, or a night-time veranda with a sickly blue light zapping the insects.

Rebecca F Kuang

author of Yellowface

I recently read and loved Anthony Doerr’s Cloud Cuckoo Land. Like David Mitchell’s Cloud Atlas, it’s a testament to ridiculous hope and the power of stories that is also ridiculously, formally ambitious – its crosscutting storylines span centuries and continents. It’s precisely the kind of book I needed to remind me how high human storytelling can soar.

Mike Gayle

author of On We Go

An MP has been murdered and a taunting message left in binary code: “Catch me if you can.” So begins Body of Lies, the politically and technically prescient conclusion to Jo Callaghan’s unique Midlands-set series featuring Kat and Lock, a human and AI detective pairing. Brimful of big ideas and heart, its action-packed finale is, to put it mildly, as moving as it is thrilling.

Bella Mackie

author of Claws Out!The Enchanted April by Elizabeth von Arnim. I read this recently and found it completely charming and brilliantly transporting. Four women, bored, lost, lonely and miserable respectively, take a villa in Italy for a month of respite. It’s funny, tender and trots along at pace. But above all else, it’s a novel about women and the community that springs up between them. A perfect beach read.

Curtis Sittenfeld

author of American WifeCrash Into Me by Robinne Lee is the ideal beach read not just because I literally was reading it on the beach earlier this week, though I was, or because the American cover features waves crashing on the sand, but because it’s an irresistible mix of glamorous, thought-provoking and sexy. Jamaican-born, New York‑raised, France-dwelling photographer Cecilia is living temporarily with her famous director husband and kids in LA when she reconnects with Anouk, a model with whom she had a complex encounter 20 years earlier. Now the two women are middle-aged and equally tempted to protect and blow up their lives. This is Lee’s follow-up to The Idea of You, and it’s just as juicy.

Harriet Tyce

author of Witch TrialNonesuch by Francis Spufford is an absolute banger. Historical meets fantastical in this London blitz-set novel. The perfect combination of literary and compulsive page-turner, it reads like a dream. A bonus recommendation for Time to Burn by Ellery Lloyd, which also starts in the blitz but adds a thoroughly contemporary, compelling time-travelling twist.

Abir Mukherjee

author of The Burning Grounds

My choice is The Shadow Step by Mark Billingham, the latest in the Blackpool-set series featuring the wisecracking, ballroom-dancing detective Declan Miller. This one sees our hero running an investigation into the murder of a rather despicable young man, which quickly gets derailed by the kidnapping of a student. As with the others in this series, Billingham weaves a fiendish plot but also lets rip with the jokes. An absolute joy to read.

Abigail Dean

author of The Death of Us

I’d recommend Main Characters by Bobby Palmer. Seb and Clara meet in a Soho square, and an epic on-again, off-again romance begins. But their story is narrated by everybody except the main characters. Sometimes it’s a close friend, but we also hear from people‑watchers, neighbours and colleagues. The result has the feeling of a short-story collection, with small, perceptive insights into a vast cast of characters, and the ways lives collide and divert. Make sure you have sunglasses to hand – I wept.

Jennie Godfrey

author of The Barbecue at No 9

This year, Dead Heat by Sabine Durrant exceeded my unofficial “beach read” criteria of 1) page-turning crime or thriller 2) set in hot weather. This elevated psychological thriller, which takes place over a Greek summer, gave me serious Patricia Highsmith vibes. It’s classy, cinematic and truly thrilling.

Shari Lapena

author of Getting Away With Murder

In Five by Ilona Bannister, someone on a London train platform will die in five minutes when the train arrives. As the clock ticks down, you meet the characters who might die, and you get to know them intimately. If you want a completely immersive read, this is for you.

Nick Harkaway

author of Karla’s Choice

If Lewis Carroll sat down with Mick Herron to write a thriller about memory and nightmare, you’d get There Is No Antimemetics Division by qntm. A funny, gripping and genuinely disturbing counter-espionage monster novel told in beach-friendly episodic style. What’s not to love?

Paula Hawkins

author of The Girl on the TrainFour Terrible Parents by Calla Henkel. Careering towards 40, two rock stars, an artist and a former banker decide the time has come to settle down, get married, and co-parent a child (while also renovating a hotel in South Carolina). Henkel’s comedy-slash-thriller is so fiendishly plotted you might not even notice all she has to say about art, love, friendship and family.

Kate Mosse

author of The Map of Bones

Recently reissued, Fenny by Lettice Cooper – first published in 1953 – is a coming-of-age story set in the Tuscan hills. Dripping with heat, the sound of cicadas and the smell of the pine trees, this is the story of a Yorkshire governess who pitches up at a villa outside Florence in the years before the second world war and falls in love with the country, the light, the Italian pace of life. Heartwarming, atmospheric, a perfect summer read.

Adele Parks

author of Just My LuckMad Mabel by Sally Hepworth. You may not have heard of this Australian-born, New York Times bestselling author yet, but I’ve been reading her for years; I love everything she’s written and I’m waiting to see her to blow-up here. Her bittersweet, thrilling dramas are shot through with life-enhancing humour. Somehow Hepworth’s Aussie sunshine floods off the page even when she’s delivering dark twists and murders. In this novel, unapologetically grumpy, fiercely independent 81-year-old Elsie lives quietly in an Australian suburb, except everywhere she goes people die in mysterious circumstances.

Claire Powell

author of All In

I couldn’t get enough of Some Bright Nowhere by Ann Packer, which is told from the perspective of a husband whose terminally ill wife asks him to move out so her best friends can move in. The literary equivalent of a friend telling an increasingly shocking story, it’s an unexpected and deeply moving read.

entries.title: Lucy Caldwell: ‘Even your text messages fizz after reading James Joyce’

entries.content:
My earliest reading memory

The summer my middle sister was born, my mum and I would walk to the shops at Cherryvalley, in east Belfast, to do her messages, and she’d buy me the latest issue of Storyteller, illustrated tales from around the world. It came with a cassette tape of actors reading the stories, a ding to tell you when to turn the page. My favourite was a Japanese folktale called The Goblin Rat. I was only just two, but I listened to it, entranced and terrified, until I could recite it by heart.

My favourite book growing up

Susan Cooper’s The Dark Is Rising series. I first read them aged 10 – I’ve read the title book every midwinter since, and read them last year with my own then-10-year-old son. They tell a haunting story of the age-old battle between the forces of dark and light, weaving in Arthurian legend, shot through with an adult melancholy that makes them as compelling now as then.

The book that made me want to be a writer

Jennifer Johnston’s How Many Miles to Babylon? We read it in English when I was 13 and our homework was to write an extra chapter. I spent every spare minute that week writing mine – the intoxicating feeling of tuning in to another world, until that world becomes more real than your own.

The book I came back to

I’ve always loved Dubliners by James Joyce, but first read Ulysses in paroxysms of undergraduate anxiety about not “getting” the references. Years later, I bought an edition with no footnotes, no endnotes, just the novel itself – it was, and continues to be, one of the most glorious reading experiences of my life. Even your text messages fizz after you’ve been reading Joyce.

The book I reread

Clarissa Pinkola Estés, Women Who Run With the Wolves. She’s a Jungian psychoanalyst and a cantadora, a keeper of the old tales, and this book is about the secret gifts and power of mythology, the paths to your inner psyche, reclaiming your wildness. I’ve read it in my 20s, 30s and 40s, and different stories have sung out to me each time. Every woman should read this book.

The book I could never read again

I love Rosamond Lehmann but I’ve never been able to get past the part in The Echoing Grove where two sisters try, ineptly and at agonising length, to bludgeon a rat to death.

The book I discovered later in life

As teenagers, we’d dare each other to leave the school library copy of Lady Chatterley’s Lover open on the “dirty bits” – where the spine was broken. But I didn’t actually read any DH Lawrence until I was in my 40s, and I’m so glad I came to that book later in life, as a wife, as a mother. It’s not the explicitness of the sex that’s shocking – it’s the ardency of the longing, the abandon of his rhythms. That would have been wasted on me before.

The book I am currently reading

I’ve just finished Helen Bain’s debut, The Daffodil Days, which I loved – an account of Sylvia Plath’s last year, told backwards, in an intricate series of stories by people momentarily close to her. It’s hard to know what to follow it up with, but I have high hopes for Courttia Newland’s The Art of Opposition, a book of essays “on hope, resilience and creative expression beyond the mainstream”, by a writer I know to be a formidably sharp and compassionate thinker.

My comfort read

It’s not that the stories themselves are comforting – far from it – but I reread Lorrie Moore’s Self-Help. There’s such pleasure in knowing that each story, like Philip Larkin’s definition of poetry, is a perfect verbal device to take you through its experience.
